sweep_summary: Swedish (swed1254) is coded 'fixed-strict' with an initial-stress rule vector although the deciding quotation (Frid 2001, restating Bruce 1993) says stress is not fixed. Of the 28 title hits, only Riad 2012 (Lingua, already listed), Myrberg & Riad 2015 (NJL) and marginally Bruce 1977 bear on word stress; the rest are tonal-accent phonetics, intonation/phrasing, sign language, L2 accent, a Gotland-dialect (Gutnish) monograph (Klintberg 1885, not found online), or duplicates. downloaded and read: Riad 2012 author postprint (49 pp, via Internet Archive copy of the DiVA full text; DiVA itself could not be reached by automated download), Myrberg & Riad 2015 (Cambridge bronze-OA PDF) and Bruce 1977 (LUP OA scan). Riad 2012 sec. 4.1 gives the current reference account: one stress per minimal prosodic word; roots tonic (lexically stressed) or unspecified; posttonic/pretonic affixes; default RIGHTMOST = 'the rightmost available syllable in the minimal prosodic word is stressed' (kalíf, elektricitét, teorí), older analyses having assumed penult default; stressed syllables obey stress-to-weight. Myrberg & Riad 2015 (pp. 118-119, 126) confirms: final-stressed simplex words (epideˈmi, elektrifiˈera, moneˈtär), no stable secondary stress, -eri 'always attracts primary stress by the phonological stress rule of Swedish'. Bruce 1977 p. 9 explicitly defers the stress rules to Linell 1972 but its examples (banan, lemonad, väninna, prinsessa) presuppose non-initial stress. Net: the 'fixed-strict'/initial headline is contradicted by every first-hand source read; the record should be reclassified as non-fixed, right-edge (rightmost available syllable by default, lexically/morphologically specified otherwise), with the quantity-sensitive sub-type hedged since Riad treats weight as following stress. Nothing unread is high priority: Bruce 2007 (De Gruyter, paywalled) and Myrberg & Riad 2013 (Peter Lang, paywalled) are low; Riad 2014 The Phonology of Swedish (OUP, not in this item list) remains the fuller version of the same account. All downloads with and a stamped addendum.

new_statements.reading: Swedish word stress is not fixed to any syllable. One primary stress per minimal prosodic word (culminativity). Placement is largely lexical-morphological: roots are either 'tonic' (carry lexical stress, mostly Germanic, e.g. grís, pyjámas) or 'unspecified' (mostly Romance/Greek loans); suffixes/prefixes are tonic, unspecified, posttonic (require the stress immediately before them: -lig, -are, -er, -or, -iker) or pretonic (be-, för-). Where no lexical specification decides, a phonological default RIGHTMOST puts stress on the last available syllable of the minimal prosodic word (kalíf, elektricitét, teorí; nat-ión > nat-ion-éll > nat-ion-al-íst), 'available' excluding posttonic suffixes; hence right-edge, final by default, with penult/antepenult surfacing before posttonic suffixes. Riad explicitly notes that earlier phonological analyses took the penult as default (p. 9) and that stressed syllables obey Stress-to-weight (heavy = V: or VC:), i.e. weight follows stress rather than conditioning it. This contradicts the catalog's 'fixed-strict' initial coding and its rule vector, agrees with the record's own right-edge the primary-stress rule, and refines Bruce 1993/Frid 2001's weight-driven three-syllable window into a lexical-specification + rightmost-default system; quantity-sensitivity should stay hedged (weight is a consequence of stress here).

The precise realisation of the tonal patterns varies across dialects (see Bruce and Gårding, 1978). In Standard Swedish, the “acute accent”, or “accent I”, has a low tone associated with the stressed syllable, while the “grave accent”, or “accent II”, has a high tone. [p. 4] ... there are, as a consequence, no short vowels in open stressed syllables in Standard Swedish. This leads furthermore to the assumption that all stressed syllables in Swedish have the same weight: they are always “heavy”. [p. 8]

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with both the catalog (Gordon: initial) and the existing Riad 2012 statement; it decides nothing about synchronic placement. It adds: (a) Swedish is a stress language with a two-way tonal accent contrast on the stressed syllable; (b) all stressed syllables (main and secondary) are heavy, which is the Stress-to-weight point already in the Riad 2012 record; (c) the historical initial-stress background (Proto-Germanic / Proto-Nordic stem-initial main stress, main-stress retraction to the initial syllable after balance). It does not touch the catalog-vs-Riad disagreement over initial vs lexical/rightmost placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The thesis is about segmental quantity, not stress placement. It states that Swedish has two tonal word accents (accent I / accent II) realised on the stressed syllable of polysyllabic words, and that every stressed syllable (main or secondary stress, via the Elert 1964 quote on p. 7) is heavy: a long vowel or a short vowel plus long consonant (complementary quantity). It never states a synchronic rule for where main stress falls in modern Swedish; its only synchronic example is penna 'pencil' 'with stress on the first syllable' (p. 7). Placement statements are historical only: Proto-Germanic 'Stress fell normally on the initial syllable' (p. 29); in early Proto-Nordic 'The main-stress position of words is marked in the lexicon, and is always stem-initial' (p. 32); after the loss of balance 'Main-stress, previously dominating two syllables, retracts to the initial syllable' (p. 34).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress is mentioned only through the Elert (1964) quotation (p. 7): 'either the vowel or the immediately following consonant in syllables with main stress or secondary stress is long', i.e. secondary-stressed syllables are also heavy. No rule for its placement.
new_statements.exceptions: None for modern stress placement. Historical: balance (jämvikt) dialects of northern/central Sweden had 'level stress' over the two syllables of a light bisyllabic stem (p. 33, citing Riad 1992 p. 172), a 'two-positional main stress' that was lost by main-stress retraction to the initial syllable (p. 34).
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis analyses the SweDia 2000 quantity corpus from 86 locations in Sweden and Swedish-speaking Finland; its general prosodic statements refer to Standard (Central) Swedish 'as spoken in the Stockholm region' (p. 5). The level-stress / balance remarks concern the historical northern and central Swedish balance dialects (sec. 4.2.3-4.2.4), and the tonal-accent realisation is said to vary across dialects (p. 4).

tone_statements.quote: Contrary to traditional assumptions, Accent I and Accent II are not considered primitive categories, nor, as in earlier generative treatments, a feature of words. Rather, the accents are described in terms of universal features of pitch, which are assigned to words whose stress patterns are fully determined. Although the pitch rules differ from one dialect to another, the stress rules are substantially the same in all dialects.
tone_statements.summary: Accent I/II as pitch features assigned on the output of stress rules; dialect-specific pitch rules.

readall_conflicts: Schaeffler 2005 introduces no new conflict: it makes no synchronic placement claim for modern Swedish, so it neither confirms nor refutes the catalog's initial-stress coding (Gordon) or the existing Riad 2012 statement (lexically specified roots with a RIGHTMOST default and posttonic suffixes), which already contradict each other on placement type. The one point where Schaeffler bears on that disagreement is weight: its 'all stressed syllables in Swedish.. are always heavy' (p. 8) agrees with Riad 2012's Stress-to-weight reading (weight follows stress rather than attracting it), so the catalog's quantity-sensitivity should stay hedged as before. Its historical statements (Proto-Germanic and Proto-Nordic stem-initial main stress, retraction to the initial syllable) describe earlier stages, not the modern language.
